At a node attaining its value from one assignment, each neighboring value has only increased, so \(L_v\) has not decreased; the caps also persist. Choose a feasible witness \(b\). Maximizing \(\sum_v a_v\) after taking componentwise maximum with \(b\) restricts to the compact box \(b_v\leq a_v\leq F_p(v)\), and hence attains a maximum. A feasible assignment exceeding that maximum in any coordinate would increase this objective by taking componentwise maximum. Consequently there is a unique componentwise greatest assignment, denoted \(a_v(p)\).

It also dominates every scalar function \(k\) obtained from (7) that lies below \(F_p\). The chord-and-tail replacement just used dominates \(k\) everywhere by convexity and the tail slope bound, and its node vector is feasible for (11). Therefore it is at most the interpolation of the greatest assignment. Define that interpolation as \(k_p(q)\): endpoint-linear on every bounded interval and \(a_v(p)+t\theta_e(p)\) on every tail. It is continuous, scalar PC by the scalar lemma, and \(k_p\leq F_p\) everywhere.

Every \(a_v(p)\) is a finite concave piecewise-affine function on \(D\), with rational gradients and real constants. To see this without an unproved parametric-LP assertion, expand all caps \(F_p(v)\) into their finite affine minima. Expand each tail minimum \(\theta_e\) in the last inequalities of (11): the weighted sum of minima is the minimum over all choices of tail pieces. Thus (11) is one finite linear system in \((a,p)\) with rational variable coefficients and real constants, together with (8). Eliminate all \(a_w\), \(w\ne v\), by the elementary elimination procedure. For fixed \(p\in D\), its section in \(a_v\) is exactly \((-\infty,a_v(p)]\), because simultaneously lowering all node values preserves the Laplacians and caps. Projected inequalities involving \(a_v\) must therefore be upper bounds; zero-coefficient inequalities concern \(D\). There is at least one upper bound from the original cap. Dividing positive rational coefficients gives
\[
 a_v(p)=\min_j(c_{v,j}+g_{v,j}(p)),\qquad g_{v,j}\text{ rational}.             \tag{12}
\]
This also proves continuity on all of \(D\), including its boundary. Tail slopes already have the same property. No assertion that the dual vertices are rational is made.

## Actual raw envelope and finite rational spatial domains

Define
\[
 Q(q,z)=\sup_{p\in D}\{k_p(q)+p(z)\}.                                    \tag{13}
\]
It is finite: \(D\) is compact and all node values and tail slopes are continuous. For each fixed \(p\), \(k_p(q)+p(z)\) satisfies every actual PCC by the scalar lemma, so its supremum does too \(take the supremum of each Jensen inequality\). Since \(k_p\leq F_p\), \(Q\leq f\).

For every raw competitor \(h\leq f\), and every rational \((q,z)\), take a touching affine support of the convex completion of the rational slice \(h(q,\cdot)\). Its covector \(p\) makes (7) finite and \(h(q,z)=k_{h,p}(q)+p(z)\). Propagation proves finiteness throughout the component; a violating ray would contradict \(h\leq f\), so \(p\in D\). The preceding greatest-assignment argument gives \(k_{h,p}\leq k_p\). Hence \(h(q,z)\leq Q(q,z)\) at all rational carrier points.

The function \(Q\) is continuous. Partition \(D\) into the common finite polyhedral chambers of all affine minima in (12) and (10). Each chamber is compact. On it \(k_p(q)+p(z)\) is affine in \(p\) on a fixed graph interval, so its maximum is attained at a chamber vertex. Let \(J\) be the finite union of all these vertices, with no rationality assumption on their coordinates. Formula (13) on each edge strip is the maximum of the corresponding finitely many real-affine functions of \((q,z)\). At graph nodes the formulas agree. This proves continuity on all of \(X\).

To extend the raw upper bound to a real point \(x\), choose any finite rational structure and its minimal cell containing \(x\). In a positive-dimensional cell, shrinking simplices with rational vertices in its relative interior enclose \(x\); they can be obtained by rationally perturbing the vertices of a small enclosing simplex in the rational affine hull. Their real barycentric coefficients give actual same-cell PCCs. Raw Jensen and continuity of \(Q\) imply \(h(x)\leq Q(x)\). A zero-dimensional cell point is already rational. No raw-competitor continuity has been used.

Apply this to \(h=\gamma-C\). Together with \(Q\leq f\leq\gamma+C\), it gives the two-sided growth bound. Consequently \(Q\) itself belongs to the competitor set (3), and all its competitors are at most \(Q\). Thus
\[
                        P_\gamma(u)=Q.                                  \tag{14}
\]
Both the global lower competitor and global upper comparison are exact, and no local raising or unproved growth gluing is invoked.

Real-affine maxima alone would not prove rational spatial domains. Here there is an additional rational-gradient mechanism. Fix \(p_0\in J\). Let \(A_v(p_0)\) be the supergradient polytope of \(a_v\) there, and let \(B_e(p_0)\) be that of \(\theta_e\). Their vertices are rational by (12). Let \(N_D(p_0)\) be the outward normal cone of \(D\), generated by rational normals by (8).

For any finite concave polyhedral \(b\), the condition that \(p_0\) maximize \(b(p)+p(z)\) over \(D\) is
\[
                    z\in-\partial^+b(p_0)+N_D(p_0).                      \tag{15}
\]
For sufficiency, a supergradient \(g\) with \(g+z\in N_D\) gives the global maximum inequality. For necessity, if \((z+\partial^+b)\cap N_D\) is empty, separate the compact polytope from the closed polyhedral cone. The separating direction \(r\) has \((g+z)(r)>0\) for every supergradient and has \(n(r)\leq0\) for every normal. It is a feasible tangent direction to \(D\); a sufficiently small step is feasible. The directional derivative, the minimum of these positive quantities, increases the objective, a contradiction. This supplies the exact optimality argument, including boundary faces.

On a bounded interval \(t\in[0,\ell]\), \(b=(1-t/\ell)a_v+(t/\ell)a_w\), so (15) describes the full maximization domain of the affine plane indexed by \(p_0\) as
\[
 z\in-(1-t/\ell)A_v(p_0)-(t/\ell)A_w(p_0)+N_D(p_0).                       \tag{16}
\]
It is the convex hull of the rational endpoint point sets \((0,-\operatorname{Vert}A_v)\), \((\ell,-\operatorname{Vert}A_w)\), plus the cone of \((0,n)\) for rational generators of \(N_D\). On a tail its domain is
\[
 t\geq0,\qquad z\in-A_v(p_0)-tB_e(p_0)+N_D(p_0),                         \tag{17}
\]
generated by the rational points \((0,-\operatorname{Vert}A_v)\) and rational rays \((1,-\operatorname{Vert}B_e)\), \((0,n)\). These descriptions remain exact at \(t=0,\ell\), at zero coefficients, and at degenerate chambers. They prove that every maximization domain is a rational spatial polyhedron, though its affine value has real coefficients.

The maximization domains of a finite affine maximum, including all their faces and removing duplicates, form a complex: intersections are equality faces of the respective maxima regions. Its faces are rational because these regions are rational polyhedra. At a graph node (16)--(17) have exactly the same fibre domain for each \(p_0\), independent of the neighboring interval, so the strip complexes glue. This gives a finite rational spatial complex for \(P\) on the actual carrier. Moreover (16) has vertices only at its two graph endpoints, and (17) only at its base; faces introduce no new vertices. Thus every possible zero-dimensional domain face of this complex lies over a node of \(V\). Edge interiors cannot carry a recursive zero-cycle coefficient. This conclusion includes all bounded-edge interiors and all tails, rather than omitting their lower-face terms.

## PAPC against all local real cycles and actual regularization

Let \(z\geq0\) be any local real balanced cycle of any positive dimension on an ordinary open \(U\subset X\), and refine to make \(P\) affine. At a tested facet \(\tau\), choose a rational \(x\in U\cap\operatorname{relint}\tau\). The cone of possible nonnegative incident weights balanced modulo \(N_\tau\) is a rational polyhedral cone, so is generated by rational vectors, by the elementary cone proof above. The divisor coefficient is linear in those weights. It suffices to test a nonnegative rational incident vector \(c_\sigma\).

Write \(S=\sum c_\sigma>0\), \(B=\sum c_\sigma n_{\sigma/\tau}\in N_{\tau,\mathbb Q}\), and use the rational inward vectors \(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S\). They need not be integral normals; they have the same positive quotient directions. For sufficiently small rational \(\varepsilon>0\), the rational points \(x_\sigma=x+\varepsilon(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S)\) belong to \(\sigma\cap U\). With coefficients \(c_\sigma/S\) their barycentre is \(x\), giving an actual PCC. Its Jensen inequality is
\[
 0\leq\sum c_\sigma[P(x_\sigma)-P(x)]
       =\varepsilon\left(\sum c_\sigma P_\sigma(n_{\sigma/\tau})-P_\tau(B)\right).
\]
This is exactly (5). The zero-weight case is zero. Rational-generation then proves the inequality for every nonnegative real incident vector, and hence for every real local cycle. Thus \(P\) is PAPC in the full required sense. Balancing proved above permits recursion, and every successive divisor is nonnegative. Its full top cycle is a finite nonnegative atomic measure on the rational domain vertices. The sequence \(P+1/j\) is PAPC in the same two-sided growth class and decreases uniformly to \(P\); its divisors agree with those of \(P\). This establishes the actual operator domain and regularization without invoking source regularity assertions.

## Two complete recursive vanishing lemmas

**Quotient vanishing.** On a local \(d\)-cycle, suppose that after subtracting an ambient affine function the PA germ is pulled back by a rational linear map to a function on a complete rational fan in a space of dimension \(q<d\). Its full top divisor is zero. Let \(T_j\) be the union of quotient fan faces of codimension at least \(j\). The first divisor vanishes off the preimage of \(T_1\), since the function is ambient affine there. Inductively, near the relative interior of a quotient face of codimension \(j-1\), the preceding cycle is supported in that face's preimage, where the function is affine on the entire supporting subspace. Extend this affine function to the ambient space; balancing makes its next divisor zero. Thus the \(j\)-th divisor is supported in the preimage of \(T_j\). Since \(T_{q+1}\) is empty, the top divisor vanishes. Rational common refinements and the local formula (5) justify this argument on every lower face, without transversality or a top-face-only measure formula.

**Lineality vanishing.** If the local carrier fan and residual function-domain fan have common nonzero rational lineality, choose their common generalized fan retaining that lineality. Every face contains it; there is no zero-dimensional face. Every recursive divisor lives on that fan, so the top zero-cycle is zero. Refinement cannot change this by the proved refinement identity. Ambient affine terms can be removed first.

## Full contact at cyclic junction fibres

Let \(x=(v,z_0)\) be any possible atom of the finite rational spatial complex for \(P\). By (16)--(17), \(v\in V\) and \(z_0\) is rational. Suppose \(P(x)<f(x)\). Define its compact exposed dual face
\[
 C_x=\{p\in D:a_v(p)+p(z_0)=P(v,z_0)\}.                                  \tag{18}
\]
It is nonempty and convex. Indeed \(a_v\) is concave, and the displayed quantity never exceeds its maximum. Formula (12) describes (18) by inequalities with rational normals \(g_{v,j}+z_0\) and real constants, together with (8). Its affine-hull direction is therefore rational: the affine hull is cut out by the inequalities that are equalities throughout the polyhedron, as seen by choosing a relative-interior point and varying in its remaining feasible directions. Their homogeneous coefficients are rational. On \(C_x\), \(a_v(p)=P(x)-p(z_0)\) is affine.

For each incident bounded edge \(e=vw\), directed away from \(v\), and each tail, put
\[
 s_e(p)=\frac{a_w(p)-a_v(p)}{\ell_e}\quad\text{or}\quad s_e(p)=\theta_e(p).
                                                                         \tag{19}
\]
On \(C_x\) these are concave continuous polyhedral functions: \(a_v\) is affine there. The vertex inequality says
\[
                           \sum_e w_es_e(p)\geq0.                         \tag{20}
\]
The local germ of \(P-P(x)\) in the outgoing strip with coordinates \(t\geq0, \zeta=z-z_0\) is exactly
\[
                  h_e(t,\zeta)=\max_{p\in C_x}\{p(\zeta)+t s_e(p)\}.       \tag{21}
\]
To justify this, use the fixed finite set \(J\) of common dual chamber vertices. All inactive planes at \(x\) have strictly positive gap, and therefore stay inactive in a sufficiently small neighbourhood. Active planes have their dual points in \(C_x\). Conversely every point of \(C_x\) belongs to a chamber and is a convex combination of its vertices; equality in the exposed maximum forces those vertices to be active, and on that chamber all terms in (19) are affine. Thus (21) follows exactly. This is a local finite-germ identity, not an assumption of raw continuity or joint-convex reconstruction.

If \(\dim C_x<m\), let \(T\subset E\) annihilate the rational direction of \(C_x\). It is nonzero and rational. Subtract the ambient affine \(p_0(z)\), with \(p_0\in C_x\). Formula (21) is invariant under \(T\) in every strip; the carrier star has \(E\), hence \(T\), as lineality. A rational function-domain fan retaining \(T\) exists: each coarsest linearity region is a convex union of finitely many rational tangent cones of the already constructed spatial complex, and hence is a rational cone; its equations are invariant under \(T\). Quotient these cones by \(T\) and lift their common rational refinement. The lineality lemma proves that the full coefficient at \(x\) is zero. This case includes all lower-dimensional exposed faces.

Now suppose \(\dim C_x=m\). For \(p\in\operatorname{int}C_x\), choose \(\eta>0\) with \(p+\eta\overline B^*\subset C_x\). Formula (18) and (13) give, for every \(y\in E\),
\[
 P(v,y)-p(y)\geq P(v,z_0)-p(z_0)+\eta\|y-z_0\|.                           \tag{22}
\]
Since \(f(v,\cdot)\geq P(v,\cdot)\) is continuous, \(f(v,y)-p(y)\) is coercive and attains its infimum. If \(a_v(p)=F_p(v)\), that infimum equals the first term on the right of (22). The strict inequality away from \(z_0\) then forces the minimum at \(z_0\) and \(f(v,z_0)=P(v,z_0)\), a contradiction. Therefore
\[
                         a_v(p)<F_p(v)\quad(p\in\operatorname{int}C_x).    \tag{23}
\]

The greatest-assignment property now implies \(L_v(a(p),p)=0\). If this Laplacian were positive, raise **only its scalar LP coordinate** \(a_v\) by a sufficiently small \(\delta>0\). The cap persists by (23). At \(v\) the Laplacian decreases by \(\delta\sum_{e=vw}w_e/\ell_e\), and at every neighboring node it increases; tail slopes are fixed. Thus feasibility persists, contradicting coordinatewise maximality. If there are no bounded incident edges, raising the coordinate does not change any Laplacian and gives the contradiction even without a positive Laplacian; in that case (23) itself is impossible. This is a finite scalar feasibility argument; it is not a local perturbation of \(P\) requiring global PC gluing.

Continuity extends the equality to all of \(C_x\):
\[
                              \sum_e w_es_e=0\quad\text{on }C_x.           \tag{24}
\]
Since each \(s_e\) is concave and all weights are strictly positive, every \(s_e\) is affine on \(C_x\). Indeed the nonnegative Jensen deficits of the individual concave functions have weighted sum zero and must each vanish. On the full-dimensional \(C_x\), choose an interior point off the finitely many affine-piece walls. Formula (12) and the rational lengths show that these affine expressions have rational \(p\)-gradients. Write
\[
                    s_e(p)=\alpha_e+p(\beta_e),\qquad\beta_e\in E_\mathbb Q.
                                                                         \tag{25}
\]
The constants \(\alpha_e\) may be real. Equation (24) says \(\sum w_e\alpha_e=0\) and \(\sum w_e\beta_e=0\).

Let \(S_v\) be the actual rational span of the primitive star directions. Its only relation is (1). Consequently there is a real linear form \(A:S_v\to\mathbb R\) with \(A(v_{v,e})=\alpha_e\), and a rational linear map \(B:S_v\to E\) with \(B(v_{v,e})=\beta_e\). Rationality follows by solving the rational direction matrix for the rational values, not by assuming ray-generated lattice saturation. Formula (21) is therefore the restriction to the entire star of
\[
                       A(s)+\operatorname{supp}_{C_x}(\zeta+B(s)).        \tag{26}
\]
After removing \(A+p_0\circ(\zeta+B(s))\), it factors through the rational map \((s,\zeta)\mapsto\zeta+B(s)\) to the \(m\)-dimensional complete space \(E\). The support function of \(C_x-p_0\) has a complete rational normal fan, because (18) has rational inequality normals; its normal cones are generated by active normals as proved above. Apply quotient vanishing with \(q=m<d=m+1\). The entire recursive coefficient at \(x\) is zero, with actual primitive indices and every intermediate lower-face contribution retained.

The proof covers every possible atom: original cyclic junctions, inserted bivalent nodes, all fibre domain faces, and tail bases. Non-node edge interiors have already been excluded by the rational-domain generator argument. No tree branch decomposition, cycle cutting, globally affine lift, or independent support extension is used. For \(m=0\) the same argument reduces to the known graph contact mechanism; the new assertion is every \(m>0\) with arbitrary nonseparable data and cycles. Since the measure is finite nonnegative and every noncontact coefficient is zero, (2) follows. The integrand is bounded by the two-sided growth inequalities, and no boundary atom is introduced: the PA operator is the finite zero-cycle on \(X\), and its explicit constant-shift regularization has exactly the same measure. Infinity and all ends have been handled in (8)--(11).

For finitely many connected components, construct \(D\), the LP, and \(P\) separately. A PCC and a local cycle stay in the component of their incident cell; the finitely many measures add and a uniform growth constant is available. This finishes the stated graph-cylinder theorem.

## Exact triangle and comparison to residual scope

For \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(1,0)\), \(C=(0,1)\), the oriented bounded primitive directions are \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(-1,1)\), \(c=(0,-1)\), all of primitive length one. The leaves \(c-a=(-1,-1)\), \(a-b=(2,-1)\), \(b-c=(-1,2)\) are primitive. At each vertex the three outgoing vectors sum to zero and have rank two. Their only relation is the strictly positive unit vector. Their local lattice spans are saturated: each star contains a pair of determinant \(\pm1\). Thus this graph meets (1) with the actual lattices, and the theorem applies to \(G\times E\) in every dimension.

The tree amalgamation failure is still genuine as a diagnostic: before imposing the cycle period, \(a,b,c\) are independent and the formal walk ends at \(a+b+c\ne0\); closing the actual graph imposes \(a+b+c=0\). ## Actual nonseparable cyclic example and exhaustive finite recursion

On the specified triangle times \(\mathbb R_z\), choose
\[
 \gamma(x,y,z)=\frac{|x|+|y|}{10}+|z|.
\]
This is the restriction of an ambient convex function and hence satisfies every actual PCC. Its end slopes in the graph direction are \(1/5,3/10,3/10\), and its vertical slopes are positive after the \(|z|\) subdivision; thus it is positive at infinity, including mixed recession directions. On each of the three A-incident edges let \(t\) be primitive distance from \(A\), and put
\[
 u(t,z)=-\frac32\max\{0,1-|z-1|-2t\};
\]
put \(u=0\) on the other edges. On the bounded A-incident edges \(t=1\) at their opposite endpoints, where the formula vanishes, so the function is globally continuous. All walls and endpoints are rational, and \(-3/2\leq u\leq0\). It is nonseparable: its values at \((t,z)=(0,1),(1/2,1),(0,0),(1/2,0)\) have nonzero rectangular difference.

Insert \(D,H,J\) at distance \(1/2\) from \(A\) along \(AB,AC\), and A's leaf, respectively. The dual domain is \([-1,1]\). \]
The candidates at \(2t\) and \(2-2t\) are no smaller than \(st\). For \(t\geq1/2\), \(u=0\), so the infimum is the graph reference value. Consequently the node caps are

 F_p(A)=\min(0,-\tfrac12-p),\quad F_p(B)=F_p(C)=\tfrac1{10},\quad

\[
\begin{split}

Directly, its Laplacian slacks at A,B,C are respectively \((2/5,1/5,1/5)\) for \(p\leq-1/2\), \((7/5+2p,-3/10-p,-3/10-p)\) for \(-1/2\leq p\leq-3/10\), and \((4/5,0,0)\) for \(p\geq-3/10\); all other slacks are zero. Use the exact formula (13), interpolating (27) on all six bounded intervals and the fixed slopes on the three tails. The common dual vertices are

## Divisor algebra with actual primitive normals

For a real PA function \(a\) and balanced real \(k\)-cycle \(z\), the divisor is
\[
 (a\cdot z)(\tau)=
 \sum_{\sigma\succ\tau}z(\sigma)a_{\sigma,\mathrm{lin}}(n_{\sigma/\tau})
 -a_{\tau,\mathrm{lin}}
       \left(\sum_{\sigma\succ\tau}z(\sigma)n_{\sigma/\tau}\right).
 \tag{2}
\]
The last argument is tangent by balancing. Altering a lift by a tangent vector makes the two terms change equally, since the linear parts agree tangentially. The formula is therefore lift-independent, real bilinear and local on ordinary opens. Ambient affine functions have zero divisor.

Refinement compatibility in the dimensions needed here follows directly from (2). At a new tested facet, take its minimal old face. If that old face has dimension larger than the cycle dimension, every inherited incident weight is zero. If it has the cycle dimension, exactly two nonzero inherited pieces meet in that plane with equal weights and affine parts and opposite quotient normals, so their terms cancel. If it has the tested facet dimension, the tangent lattice and incident primitive normal classes are the old ones, and the coefficient is inherited unchanged. Extra incident pieces have zero inherited weight. These cases also preserve balancing of a subdivided cycle. Applying the same argument successively to the first divisor proves refinement compatibility of the second divisor. In particular, inserting vertices in an affine edge produces opposite slopes with identical edge weights and coefficient zero; inserting a vertex inside an affine top cell produces zero first divisor there.

For completeness, balancing of the first divisor of a two-cycle is also elementary. Translate the tested vertex to zero and use a pointed rational local two-fan; harmless rational cuts can make any local lineality pointed. Let \(r,s\) be the primitive boundary vectors of a two-cone. Its saturated plane lattice \(N_C\) has index
\[
 \chi_{rs}=[N_C:\mathbb Zr+\mathbb Zs].
\]
The primitive quotient normal at \(r\) is represented modulo \(\mathbb Rr\) by \(s/\chi_{rs}\): extend primitive \(r\) to a basis of \(N_C\), in which the transverse coordinate of \(s\) has absolute value \(\chi_{rs}\). The representative need not itself be an integral lift; their tangential difference cancels in (2). If cone weights are \(\omega_{rs}\), top balancing gives
\[
 \sum_{C_{rs}\succ r}\frac{\omega_{rs}}{\chi_{rs}}s=t_r r,
 \qquad
 D_a(r)=\sum_{C_{rs}\succ r}\frac{\omega_{rs}}{\chi_{rs}}a(s)-t_ra(r).
 \tag{3}
\]
Here \(a\) is the homogeneous germ after subtracting its value at the vertex. Multiplying \(D_a(r)\) by \(r\) and summing, the first sum is the sum, once for each unordered cone, of
\(\omega_{rs}(a(s)r+a(r)s)/\chi_{rs}\). Replacing \(t_rr\) by its balancing sum in the subtracted term gives exactly the same sum. Thus \(\sum_rD_a(r)r=0\), proving that the first divisor is a real one-cycle. Its complete second coefficient at the vertex is
\[
                      (a^2\cdot[X])\{0\}=\sum_rD_a(r)a(r).
 \tag{4}
\]
This includes every first-divisor face, including original branching axes and newly created diagonal faces.

The normalization is the intersection normalization. On a unit-weight complete plane, \(a(s,t)=|s|+|t|\) has first weight two on each of the four coordinate rays and germ value one on each primitive ray. Formula (4) gives eight, which is \(2!\) times the area four of the slope square. We use (2)--(4) themselves, not an Alexandrov substitution at singular junctions.

We need a finite polyhedron fact to propagate those bounds without raw continuity. Every nonempty pointed rational polyhedron \(\sigma\) is

where the \(v_i\) are rational vertices and the \(r_j\) are rational recession vectors; \(a\geq1\), and \(b\) may be zero. Here is a proof. At the shared centre \((v,1/2)\) and rational branch endpoints \((\varepsilon u_i,1/2)\) with coefficients \(1/3\), the centre is one and the mean is \(1-\varepsilon/3\). For \(\varepsilon=1/4\) the endpoint values are \(7/8,7/8,1\), mean \(11/12\), defect \(1/12\). Their barycentre is the centre, and the star product rectangles are actual cofaces; thus this is an actual failed PCC. A node assignment dominating both original corner arrays under their maximum caps would have to be their coordinatewise maximum, whose roofs fail this test. Consequently that roof-feasible finite-node set has no greatest assignment under those caps. The actual functional maximum has trace \(\max\{1-t,t\}\), with an additional fibre break. This diagnostic invalidates that coarse reconstruction scheme; by itself it is not a regularity or contact counterexample. The cyclic counterexample (5)--(12) supplies the new contact conclusion separately.

The main checks are: actual graph/product balancing; finite rational walls; recession-vector growth; all real PCC tests for the candidate; all local real-cycle PAPC tests; the zero-vertex PCC; finite pointed-cell generation; raw comparison with remote rational endpoints and real centres; explicit decreasing uniform regularization; actual primitive indices in the full two-stage recursion; and the zero gap at every other original operator vertex. All these checks are arguments in this file, not grants from source documents.

No statement is made that every raw envelope on this pair is PA, continuous or regularizable. No all-reference negative theorem is claimed. A general localization to arbitrary finite graphs and arbitrary real references would need its own growth-preserving construction and rational-domain proof. 41: We record proofs of the finite-dimensional facts used subsequently. A cone defined by finitely many rational inequalities has finitely many rational generators. Remove its rational lineality first. In the pointed quotient the sum of the defining nonnegative forms is positive away from zero; its section of value one is bounded, since an unbounded sequence normalized on the sphere would give a nonzero vector of value zero. A bounded polyhedron is the convex hull of its finitely many vertices: within the minimal face of any nonvertex point, a line through the point ends on smaller-dimensional faces, and induction reduces to vertices. Vertices solve full-rank subsystems, hence are rational for rational data. Lift back and add both signs of a rational lineality basis.

Thus the graph projection is in a single straight edge chain through bivalent vertices, or is a vertex. This applies to every permitted rational structure, not just our chosen subdivision.

98: **Scalar lemma.** Suppose \(k\) is finite on rational graph points and satisfies rational graph PCC inequalities with rational coefficients. It has a continuous completion, is convex on every edge, has finite outgoing derivatives \(s_{v,e}\), and satisfies \(\sum_e w_es_{v,e}\geq0\). Conversely a continuous function convex on the edges with these inequalities, when added to any affine function of \(E\), satisfies every actual cylinder PCC, with real coefficients and all real centres.

100: For the first assertion, complete the rational Jensen function on each edge interior. A one-sided limit at an endpoint is finite and at most the specified endpoint value: an endpoint secant bounds it above and an interior secant bounds it below. For rational small \(t>0\), the points \(v+t v_{v,e}\) with coefficients \(w_e/\sum w_e\) are an actual vertex PCC. Its inequality and the endpoint upper bounds force all limits to equal \(k(v)\). Every outgoing derivative is bounded above by a finite secant. Dividing the same PCC inequality by \(t\) prevents any derivative being \(-\infty\), and gives the weighted derivative inequality.
101: 
102: For the converse, edgewise convexity and the bivalent inequalities give ordinary convexity on every straight chain. At a branching centre \(v\), group the graph displacements of any cylinder PCC as \(t_i v_{v,e}\), with \(t_i\geq0\), using the preceding structural observation. Their weighted sum is zero, so the group coefficients \(b_e=\sum_{i\text{ in }e}\alpha_it_i\) equal \(cw_e\), \(c\geq0\). Convexity gives \(k(q_i)-k(v)\geq t_i s_{v,e}\). Summing gives a nonnegative result. At a centre in a straight chain the assertion is ordinary convexity. Terms with zero graph displacement and the affine \(E\) terms are handled by the barycentre identity. This proves every actual PCC directly, including remote endpoints, irrational centres, and structures crossing bivalent subdivision points. No open-cover locality theorem is used.

104: For a raw cylinder competitor \(h\), its rational slice at a rational graph point \(q\) has the finite convex completion just proved. For a real dual covector \(p\in E^*\), put
105: \[
106:  k_{h,p}(q)=\inf_{z\in E_\mathbb Q}(h(q,z)-p(z))\in[-\infty,\infty).             \tag{7}
107: \]
108: It satisfies rational graph PCC inequalities: choose rational \(z_i\) approaching the endpoint infima, apply the actual cylinder PCC at \((q,\sum_i\alpha_i z_i)\), subtract \(p\), and take the infimum. Rational coefficients ensure that this last affine coordinate is rational. If one endpoint has infimum \(-\infty\), vary that endpoint alone.

110: If (7) is finite at one rational graph point, it is finite at every rational point in that connected component. From an edge-interior finite centre, any other rational point on that edge can be an endpoint in a rational combination by choosing the other endpoint on the opposite side. At a finite vertex, any rational remote point \(v+t_ev_{v,e}\) on a chosen incident edge belongs to a vertex PCC with positive rational coefficients proportional to \(w_e/t_e\), choosing positive rational distances within all other incident edges. No endpoint can have value \(-\infty\). Propagate across the finite connected graph. This works through cycles and all unbounded ends. The scalar lemma then applies to (7).

112: ## Finite partial-infimum data, with tails and recession constraints
113: 
114: Work in one connected component, identify \(E\) rationally with its lattice vector space, and take a common finite rational affine structure for \(f=\gamma+u\) and \(\gamma\), refined by the original edge strips. Each cell is pointed: a nonzero lineality direction would give two opposite reference recession slopes, incompatible with positivity at infinity. Formula (4) therefore applies.
115: 
116: For each cell ray with zero graph coordinate, write its affine obstacle slope as \(s_r\) and its \(E\)-coordinate as \(r_E\), and define
117: \[
118:  D=\{p\in E^*:p(r_E)\leq s_r\text{ for every such ray}\}.                    \tag{8}
119: \]
120: All inequality normals are rational; constants may be real. On every recession ray \(u\) has zero slope, by boundedness, so (8) is the same for \(f\) and \(\gamma\). It contains 0 in its interior, because every nonzero vertical ray has strictly positive reference slope. For \(m=0\), \(D=\{0\}\) in the zero-dimensional dual space.
121: 
122: Set \(F_p(q)=\inf_{z\in E}(f(q,z)-p(z))\). For \(p\in D\) this is finite at every \(q\) and its infimum is attained at a vertex of some cell fibre. Indeed, the fibre is pointed and its recession cone is generated by the zero-graph cell rays: graph recession is zero on bounded strips and nonnegative on unbounded strips, so a zero-graph combination cannot use any positive-graph ray. The objective is nonnegative on this recession cone, and (4) for the fibre gives a minimizing vertex. There are finitely many cells. If \(p\notin D\), a violating rational ray based at a rational point gives \(F_p(q)=-\infty\) at a rational graph point. Thus (8) is precisely the common finite domain required here.
123: 
124: The set \(D\) is compact. At any fixed rational graph vertex, the finite-PA function \(f(q,z)\) is bounded above by \(M\|z\|+B\), for some finite \(M,B\) (use finitely many affine pieces and the dual norm). If \(\|p\|>M\), a direction with \(p(z)>M\|z\|\) makes the infimum \(-\infty\). Finiteness for \(p\in D\) bounds \(D\). This proof does not require \(f\) convex.
125: 
126: Subdivide each bounded edge at the graph coordinates of all its spatial cell vertices, and each end at those coordinates and its original base. This is finite and rational. Between consecutive coordinates a fibre vertex lies on a spatial one-face: the minimal face containing it loses one dimension under the slicing hyperplane, so has dimension at most one. A one-face traversing the interval has rational form \(z(t)=z_i+t b_i\), and obstacle height real-affine in \(t\). Its feasibility across that open interval is constant, because changes occur only at projected spatial vertices. Therefore on each such interval
127: \[
128:  F_p(t)=\min_i\{A_i(p)+t B_i(p)\},                      \tag{9}
129: \]
130: where the finite index set is independent of \(p\); \(A_i,B_i\) are affine in \(p\), with rational linear coefficients and real constants. At a node \(v\), slicing the cells directly gives \(F_p(v)\) as a finite minimum of affine functions of \(p\), again with rational gradients and real constants.
131: 
132: For clarity, (9) extends concavely and continuously to each finite interval endpoint. Its candidate fibre vertices have finite limits there, so their limiting objective values are at least \(F_p(v)\). Conversely, fixing any finite \(z\) and using continuity of \(f(t,z)\) gives \(\limsup_{t\to v}F_p(t)\leq f(v,z)-p(z)\); then take its infimum over \(z\). This proves equality of the limits. It also proves branchwise continuity at a graph vertex. The possibility of a different endpoint fibre type is not discarded.
133: 
134: After the last projected vertex on an end, translate its primitive parameter to start at 0. Formula (9) holds for all \(t\geq0\), and
135: \[
136:  \theta_e(p):=\lim_{t\to\infty}F_p(t)/t=\min_i B_i(p),\qquad
137:  F_p(t)-\theta_e(p)t\text{ is nondecreasing}.             \tag{10}
138: \]
139: Every \(B_i-\theta_e\geq0\) proves the monotonicity term by term. In particular the line from any value at most \(F_p(0)\) with slope \(\theta_e(p)\) lies below the entire tail obstacle. All recession constraints and finite endpoints have now been retained.

141: ## The graph incidence polyhedron and its greatest assignment
142: 
143: Let \(V\) be the finite node set just obtained. For fixed \(p\in D\), introduce node values \(a_v\), and impose
144: \[
145:  a_v\leq F_p(v),\qquad
146:  L_v(a,p):=\sum_{e=vw\text{ bounded}}\frac{w_e}{\ell_e}(a_w-a_v)
147:                 +\sum_{e\text{ tail at }v}w_e\theta_e(p)\geq0.             \tag{11}
148: \]
149: Here \(\ell_e>0\) is the actual rational primitive length. All bounded edges are present in this one system, including each edge of every cycle. Do not integrate a graph direction into a larger lift or unwind the graph.
150: 
151: There is a feasible assignment. The raw PC function \(\gamma-C\), \(C=\|u\|_\infty\), lies below \(f\). Its partial infimum is finite for \(p\in D\), by (8) applied to \(\gamma\), and the scalar lemma applies. Replace its restriction on each bounded interval by its endpoint chord, and on each tail by the line of slope \(\theta_e(p)\) from its endpoint value. Convexity and the upper bound \(F_p\) show that the chords lie below the concave data (9); the tail bound follows from (10). The chord outgoing slopes at both endpoints are at least the old outgoing derivatives. On a tail the asymptotic upper bound by (9) forces every secant slope of the old convex function to be at most \(\theta_e(p)\), so the new outgoing slope is also at least the old one. Thus all inequalities in (11) hold.
152: 
153: The componentwise maximum of two feasible assignments is feasible. At a node attaining its value from one assignment, each neighboring value has only increased, so \(L_v\) has not decreased; the caps also persist. Choose a feasible witness \(b\). Maximizing \(\sum_v a_v\) after taking componentwise maximum with \(b\) restricts to the compact box \(b_v\leq a_v\leq F_p(v)\), and hence attains a maximum. A feasible assignment exceeding that maximum in any coordinate would increase this objective by taking componentwise maximum. Consequently there is a unique componentwise greatest assignment, denoted \(a_v(p)\).
154: 
155: It also dominates every scalar function \(k\) obtained from (7) that lies below \(F_p\). The chord-and-tail replacement just used dominates \(k\) everywhere by convexity and the tail slope bound, and its node vector is feasible for (11). Therefore it is at most the interpolation of the greatest assignment. Define that interpolation as \(k_p(q)\): endpoint-linear on every bounded interval and \(a_v(p)+t\theta_e(p)\) on every tail. It is continuous, scalar PC by the scalar lemma, and \(k_p\leq F_p\) everywhere.
156: 
157: Every \(a_v(p)\) is a finite concave piecewise-affine function on \(D\), with rational gradients and real constants. To see this without an unproved parametric-LP assertion, expand all caps \(F_p(v)\) into their finite affine minima. Expand each tail minimum \(\theta_e\) in the last inequalities of (11): the weighted sum of minima is the minimum over all choices of tail pieces. Thus (11) is one finite linear system in \((a,p)\) with rational variable coefficients and real constants, together with (8). Eliminate all \(a_w\), \(w\ne v\), by the elementary elimination procedure. For fixed \(p\in D\), its section in \(a_v\) is exactly \((-\infty,a_v(p)]\), because simultaneously lowering all node values preserves the Laplacians and caps. Projected inequalities involving \(a_v\) must therefore be upper bounds; zero-coefficient inequalities concern \(D\). There is at least one upper bound from the original cap. Dividing positive rational coefficients gives
158: \[
159:  a_v(p)=\min_j(c_{v,j}+g_{v,j}(p)),\qquad g_{v,j}\text{ rational}.             \tag{12}
160: \]
161: This also proves continuity on all of \(D\), including its boundary. Tail slopes already have the same property. No assertion that the dual vertices are rational is made.

163: ## Actual raw envelope and finite rational spatial domains
164: 
165: Define
166: \[
167:  Q(q,z)=\sup_{p\in D}\{k_p(q)+p(z)\}.                                    \tag{13}
168: \]
169: It is finite: \(D\) is compact and all node values and tail slopes are continuous. For each fixed \(p\), \(k_p(q)+p(z)\) satisfies every actual PCC by the scalar lemma, so its supremum does too \(take the supremum of each Jensen inequality\). Since \(k_p\leq F_p\), \(Q\leq f\).

171: For every raw competitor \(h\leq f\), and every rational \((q,z)\), take a touching affine support of the convex completion of the rational slice \(h(q,\cdot)\). Its covector \(p\) makes (7) finite and \(h(q,z)=k_{h,p}(q)+p(z)\). Propagation proves finiteness throughout the component; a violating ray would contradict \(h\leq f\), so \(p\in D\). The preceding greatest-assignment argument gives \(k_{h,p}\leq k_p\). Hence \(h(q,z)\leq Q(q,z)\) at all rational carrier points.

173: The function \(Q\) is continuous. Partition \(D\) into the common finite polyhedral chambers of all affine minima in (12) and (10). Each chamber is compact. On it \(k_p(q)+p(z)\) is affine in \(p\) on a fixed graph interval, so its maximum is attained at a chamber vertex. Let \(J\) be the finite union of all these vertices, with no rationality assumption on their coordinates. Formula (13) on each edge strip is the maximum of the corresponding finitely many real-affine functions of \((q,z)\). At graph nodes the formulas agree. This proves continuity on all of \(X\).
174: 
175: To extend the raw upper bound to a real point \(x\), choose any finite rational structure and its minimal cell containing \(x\). In a positive-dimensional cell, shrinking simplices with rational vertices in its relative interior enclose \(x\); they can be obtained by rationally perturbing the vertices of a small enclosing simplex in the rational affine hull. Their real barycentric coefficients give actual same-cell PCCs. Raw Jensen and continuity of \(Q\) imply \(h(x)\leq Q(x)\). A zero-dimensional cell point is already rational. No raw-competitor continuity has been used.

177: Apply this to \(h=\gamma-C\). Together with \(Q\leq f\leq\gamma+C\), it gives the two-sided growth bound. Consequently \(Q\) itself belongs to the competitor set (3), and all its competitors are at most \(Q\). Thus
178: \[
179:                         P_\gamma(u)=Q.                                  \tag{14}
180: \]
181: Both the global lower competitor and global upper comparison are exact, and no local raising or unproved growth gluing is invoked.

183: Real-affine maxima alone would not prove rational spatial domains. Here there is an additional rational-gradient mechanism. Fix \(p_0\in J\). Let \(A_v(p_0)\) be the supergradient polytope of \(a_v\) there, and let \(B_e(p_0)\) be that of \(\theta_e\). Their vertices are rational by (12). Let \(N_D(p_0)\) be the outward normal cone of \(D\), generated by rational normals by (8).

185: For any finite concave polyhedral \(b\), the condition that \(p_0\) maximize \(b(p)+p(z)\) over \(D\) is
186: \[
187:                     z\in-\partial^+b(p_0)+N_D(p_0).                      \tag{15}
188: \]
189: For sufficiency, a supergradient \(g\) with \(g+z\in N_D\) gives the global maximum inequality. For necessity, if \((z+\partial^+b)\cap N_D\) is empty, separate the compact polytope from the closed polyhedral cone. The separating direction \(r\) has \((g+z)(r)>0\) for every supergradient and has \(n(r)\leq0\) for every normal. It is a feasible tangent direction to \(D\); a sufficiently small step is feasible. The directional derivative, the minimum of these positive quantities, increases the objective, a contradiction. This supplies the exact optimality argument, including boundary faces.

191: On a bounded interval \(t\in[0,\ell]\), \(b=(1-t/\ell)a_v+(t/\ell)a_w\), so (15) describes the full maximization domain of the affine plane indexed by \(p_0\) as
192: \[
193:  z\in-(1-t/\ell)A_v(p_0)-(t/\ell)A_w(p_0)+N_D(p_0).                       \tag{16}
194: \]
195: It is the convex hull of the rational endpoint point sets \((0,-\operatorname{Vert}A_v)\), \((\ell,-\operatorname{Vert}A_w)\), plus the cone of \((0,n)\) for rational generators of \(N_D\). On a tail its domain is

198: \]

These descriptions remain exact at \(t=0,\ell\), at zero coefficients, and at degenerate chambers. They prove that every maximization domain is a rational spatial polyhedron, though its affine value has real coefficients.

201: The maximization domains of a finite affine maximum, including all their faces and removing duplicates, form a complex: intersections are equality faces of the respective maxima regions. Its faces are rational because these regions are rational polyhedra. At a graph node (16)--(17) have exactly the same fibre domain for each \(p_0\), independent of the neighboring interval, so the strip complexes glue. This gives a finite rational spatial complex for \(P\) on the actual carrier. Moreover (16) has vertices only at its two graph endpoints, and (17) only at its base; faces introduce no new vertices. Thus every possible zero-dimensional domain face of this complex lies over a node of \(V\). Edge interiors cannot carry a recursive zero-cycle coefficient. This conclusion includes all bounded-edge interiors and all tails, rather than omitting their lower-face terms.

203: ## PAPC against all local real cycles and actual regularization
204: 
205: Let \(z\geq0\) be any local real balanced cycle of any positive dimension on an ordinary open \(U\subset X\), and refine to make \(P\) affine. At a tested facet \(\tau\), choose a rational \(x\in U\cap\operatorname{relint}\tau\). The cone of possible nonnegative incident weights balanced modulo \(N_\tau\) is a rational polyhedral cone, so is generated by rational vectors, by the elementary cone proof above. The divisor coefficient is linear in those weights. It suffices to test a nonnegative rational incident vector \(c_\sigma\).
206: 
207: Write \(S=\sum c_\sigma>0\), \(B=\sum c_\sigma n_{\sigma/\tau}\in N_{\tau,\mathbb Q}\), and use the rational inward vectors \(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S\). They need not be integral normals; they have the same positive quotient directions. For sufficiently small rational \(\varepsilon>0\), the rational points \(x_\sigma=x+\varepsilon(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S)\) belong to \(\sigma\cap U\). With coefficients \(c_\sigma/S\) their barycentre is \(x\), giving an actual PCC. Its Jensen inequality is
208: \[
209:  0\leq\sum c_\sigma[P(x_\sigma)-P(x)]
210:        =\varepsilon\left(\sum c_\sigma P_\sigma(n_{\sigma/\tau})-P_\tau(B)\right).
211: \]
212: This is exactly (5). The zero-weight case is zero. Rational-generation then proves the inequality for every nonnegative real incident vector, and hence for every real local cycle. Thus \(P\) is PAPC in the full required sense. Balancing proved above permits recursion, and every successive divisor is nonnegative. Its full top cycle is a finite nonnegative atomic measure on the rational domain vertices. The sequence \(P+1/j\) is PAPC in the same two-sided growth class and decreases uniformly to \(P\); its divisors agree with those of \(P\). This establishes the actual operator domain and regularization without invoking source regularity assertions.

214: ## Two complete recursive vanishing lemmas
215: 
216: **Quotient vanishing.** On a local \(d\)-cycle, suppose that after subtracting an ambient affine function the PA germ is pulled back by a rational linear map to a function on a complete rational fan in a space of dimension \(q<d\). Its full top divisor is zero. Let \(T_j\) be the union of quotient fan faces of codimension at least \(j\). The first divisor vanishes off the preimage of \(T_1\), since the function is ambient affine there. Inductively, near the relative interior of a quotient face of codimension \(j-1\), the preceding cycle is supported in that face's preimage, where the function is affine on the entire supporting subspace. Extend this affine function to the ambient space; balancing makes its next divisor zero. Thus the \(j\)-th divisor is supported in the preimage of \(T_j\). Since \(T_{q+1}\) is empty, the top divisor vanishes. Rational common refinements and the local formula (5) justify this argument on every lower face, without transversality or a top-face-only measure formula.
217: 
218: **Lineality vanishing.** If the local carrier fan and residual function-domain fan have common nonzero rational lineality, choose their common generalized fan retaining that lineality. Every face contains it; there is no zero-dimensional face. Every recursive divisor lives on that fan, so the top zero-cycle is zero. Refinement cannot change this by the proved refinement identity. Ambient affine terms can be removed first.

220: ## Full contact at cyclic junction fibres
221: 
222: Let \(x=(v,z_0)\) be any possible atom of the finite rational spatial complex for \(P\). By (16)--(17), \(v\in V\) and \(z_0\) is rational. Suppose \(P(x)<f(x)\). Define its compact exposed dual face
223: \[
224:  C_x=\{p\in D:a_v(p)+p(z_0)=P(v,z_0)\}.                                  \tag{18}
225: \]
226: It is nonempty and convex. Indeed \(a_v\) is concave, and the displayed quantity never exceeds its maximum. Formula (12) describes (18) by inequalities with rational normals \(g_{v,j}+z_0\) and real constants, together with (8). Its affine-hull direction is therefore rational: the affine hull is cut out by the inequalities that are equalities throughout the polyhedron, as seen by choosing a relative-interior point and varying in its remaining feasible directions. Their homogeneous coefficients are rational. On \(C_x\), \(a_v(p)=P(x)-p(z_0)\) is affine.
227: 
228: For each incident bounded edge \(e=vw\), directed away from \(v\), and each tail, put
229: \[
230:  s_e(p)=\frac{a_w(p)-a_v(p)}{\ell_e}\quad\text{or}\quad s_e(p)=\theta_e(p).
231:                                                                          \tag{19}
232: \]
233: On \(C_x\) these are concave continuous polyhedral functions: \(a_v\) is affine there. The vertex inequality says
234: \[
235:                            \sum_e w_es_e(p)\geq0.                         \tag{20}
236: \]
237: The local germ of \(P-P(x)\) in the outgoing strip with coordinates \(t\geq0, \zeta=z-z_0\) is exactly
238: \[
239:                   h_e(t,\zeta)=\max_{p\in C_x}\{p(\zeta)+t s_e(p)\}.       \tag{21}
240: \]
241: To justify this, use the fixed finite set \(J\) of common dual chamber vertices. All inactive planes at \(x\) have strictly positive gap, and therefore stay inactive in a sufficiently small neighbourhood. Active planes have their dual points in \(C_x\). Conversely every point of \(C_x\) belongs to a chamber and is a convex combination of its vertices; equality in the exposed maximum forces those vertices to be active, and on that chamber all terms in (19) are affine. Thus (21) follows exactly. This is a local finite-germ identity, not an assumption of raw continuity or joint-convex reconstruction.

243: If \(\dim C_x<m\), let \(T\subset E\) annihilate the rational direction of \(C_x\). It is nonzero and rational. Subtract the ambient affine \(p_0(z)\), with \(p_0\in C_x\). Formula (21) is invariant under \(T\) in every strip; the carrier star has \(E\), hence \(T\), as lineality. A rational function-domain fan retaining \(T\) exists: each coarsest linearity region is a convex union of finitely many rational tangent cones of the already constructed spatial complex, and hence is a rational cone; its equations are invariant under \(T\). Quotient these cones by \(T\) and lift their common rational refinement. The lineality lemma proves that the full coefficient at \(x\) is zero. This case includes all lower-dimensional exposed faces.

245: Now suppose \(\dim C_x=m\). For \(p\in\operatorname{int}C_x\), choose \(\eta>0\) with \(p+\eta\overline B^*\subset C_x\). Formula (18) and (13) give, for every \(y\in E\),
246: \[
247:  P(v,y)-p(y)\geq P(v,z_0)-p(z_0)+\eta\|y-z_0\|.                           \tag{22}
248: \]
249: Since \(f(v,\cdot)\geq P(v,\cdot)\) is continuous, \(f(v,y)-p(y)\) is coercive and attains its infimum. If \(a_v(p)=F_p(v)\), that infimum equals the first term on the right of (22). The strict inequality away from \(z_0\) then forces the minimum at \(z_0\) and \(f(v,z_0)=P(v,z_0)\), a contradiction. Therefore
250: \[
251:                          a_v(p)<F_p(v)\quad(p\in\operatorname{int}C_x).    \tag{23}
252: \]

254: The greatest-assignment property now implies \(L_v(a(p),p)=0\). If this Laplacian were positive, raise **only its scalar LP coordinate** \(a_v\) by a sufficiently small \(\delta>0\). The cap persists by (23). At \(v\) the Laplacian decreases by \(\delta\sum_{e=vw}w_e/\ell_e\), and at every neighboring node it increases; tail slopes are fixed. Thus feasibility persists, contradicting coordinatewise maximality. If there are no bounded incident edges, raising the coordinate does not change any Laplacian and gives the contradiction even without a positive Laplacian; in that case (23) itself is impossible. This is a finite scalar feasibility argument; it is not a local perturbation of \(P\) requiring global PC gluing.

256: Continuity extends the equality to all of \(C_x\):
257: \[
258:                               \sum_e w_es_e=0\quad\text{on }C_x.           \tag{24}
259: \]

Indeed the nonnegative Jensen deficits of the individual concave functions have weighted sum zero and must each vanish. On the full-dimensional \(C_x\), choose an interior point off the finitely many affine-piece walls. Formula (12) and the rational lengths show that these affine expressions have rational \(p\)-gradients. Write
261: \[
262:                     s_e(p)=\alpha_e+p(\beta_e),\qquad\beta_e\in E_\mathbb Q.
263:                                                                          \tag{25}
264: \]

267: Let \(S_v\) be the actual rational span of the primitive star directions. Its only relation is (1). Consequently there is a real linear form \(A:S_v\to\mathbb R\) with \(A(v_{v,e})=\alpha_e\), and a rational linear map \(B:S_v\to E\) with \(B(v_{v,e})=\beta_e\). Rationality follows by solving the rational direction matrix for the rational values, not by assuming ray-generated lattice saturation. Formula (21) is therefore the restriction to the entire star of
268: \[
269:                        A(s)+\operatorname{supp}_{C_x}(\zeta+B(s)).        \tag{26}
270: \]

The support function of \(C_x-p_0\) has a complete rational normal fan, because (18) has rational inequality normals; its normal cones are generated by active normals as proved above. Apply quotient vanishing with \(q=m<d=m+1\). The entire recursive coefficient at \(x\) is zero, with actual primitive indices and every intermediate lower-face contribution retained.

273: The proof covers every possible atom: original cyclic junctions, inserted bivalent nodes, all fibre domain faces, and tail bases. Non-node edge interiors have already been excluded by the rational-domain generator argument. No tree branch decomposition, cycle cutting, globally affine lift, or independent support extension is used. For \(m=0\) the same argument reduces to the known graph contact mechanism; the new assertion is every \(m>0\) with arbitrary nonseparable data and cycles. Since the measure is finite nonnegative and every noncontact coefficient is zero, (2) follows. The integrand is bounded by the two-sided growth inequalities, and no boundary atom is introduced: the PA operator is the finite zero-cycle on \(X\), and its explicit constant-shift regularization has exactly the same measure. Infinity and all ends have been handled in (8)--(11).

277: ## Exact triangle and comparison to residual scope

285: ## Actual nonseparable cyclic example and exhaustive finite recursion
286: 
287: On the specified triangle times \(\mathbb R_z\), choose
288: \[
289:  \gamma(x,y,z)=\frac{|x|+|y|}{10}+|z|.
290: \]
291: This is the restriction of an ambient convex function and hence satisfies every actual PCC. Its end slopes in the graph direction are \(1/5,3/10,3/10\), and its vertical slopes are positive after the \(|z|\) subdivision; thus it is positive at infinity, including mixed recession directions. On each of the three A-incident edges let \(t\) be primitive distance from \(A\), and put
292: \[
293:  u(t,z)=-\frac32\max\{0,1-|z-1|-2t\};
294: \]
295: put \(u=0\) on the other edges. On the bounded A-incident edges \(t=1\) at their opposite endpoints, where the formula vanishes, so the function is globally continuous. All walls and endpoints are rational, and \(-3/2\leq u\leq0\). It is nonseparable: its values at \((t,z)=(0,1),(1/2,1),(0,0),(1/2,0)\) have nonzero rectangular difference.
296: 
297: Insert \(D,H,J\) at distance \(1/2\) from \(A\) along \(AB,AC\), and A's leaf, respectively. The dual domain is \([-1,1]\). For \(0\leq t\leq1/2\) on an A-incident edge with graph reference slope \(s\in\{1/10,1/10,1/5\}\), fibre vertices occur at \(z=0,2t,1,2-2t\). Comparing their values of \(f-pz\), for \(-1\leq p\leq1\), gives
298: \[
299:  F_p(t)=\min\{st,(s+3)t-\tfrac12-p\}.
300: \]
301: The candidates at \(2t\) and \(2-2t\) are no smaller than \(st\). For \(t\geq1/2\), \(u=0\), so the infimum is the graph reference value. Consequently the node caps are
302: \[
303:  F_p(A)=\min(0,-\tfrac12-p),\quad F_p(B)=F_p(C)=\tfrac1{10},\quad
304:  F_p(D)=F_p(H)=\tfrac1{20},\quad F_p(J)=\tfrac1{10}.
305: \]
306: The greatest feasible values of the complete six-node cyclic system are
307: \[
308: \begin{split}
309:  a_A&=\min(0,-\tfrac12-p),\\
310:  a_B=a_C&=\min(\tfrac1{10},-\tfrac15-p),\\
311:  a_D=a_H&=\min(\tfrac1{20},-\tfrac15-\tfrac p2,-\tfrac7{20}-p),\\
312:  a_J&=\min(\tfrac1{10},-\tfrac25-p).
313: \end{split}                                                       \tag{27}
314: \]
315: Here is a direct greatest-assignment check, not just an LP execution. For every feasible vector, bivalent inequalities give \(a_D\leq(a_A+a_B)/2\), \(a_H\leq(a_A+a_C)/2\), and \(a_J\leq a_A+1/10\). The B and C inequalities and those bounds imply \(2a_B-a_C\leq a_A+3/10\), \(2a_C-a_B\leq a_A+3/10\). Substitution yields \(a_B,a_C\leq a_A+3/10\); combine with their caps and A's cap, then bound D,H,J. These are exactly the coordinate upper bounds in (27). The displayed vector attains all those bounds simultaneously. Directly, its Laplacian slacks at A,B,C are respectively \((2/5,1/5,1/5)\) for \(p\leq-1/2\), \((7/5+2p,-3/10-p,-3/10-p)\) for \(-1/2\leq p\leq-3/10\), and \((4/5,0,0)\) for \(p\geq-3/10\); all other slacks are zero. ## The graph incidence polyhedron and its greatest assignment

Every \(a_v(p)\) is a finite concave piecewise-affine function on \(D\), with rational gradients and real constants. \section{Local positivity and the CLD--Gubler--Rabinoff frontier}

\subsection{Positive real PL currents and residue nefness}
\label{sec:ch72-resolved-current-residue}

The problem formerly listed here is resolved in the natural
Chambert--Loir--Ducros framework.  If $X$ is a good, separated,
boundaryless, pure-dimensional strict analytic space and $h$ is real PL,
then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \dprimeddprime[h]\geq0
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 L_h(x)\text{ is nef for every }x,\\
 L_h(x)\text{ is nef for every }x
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 h\text{ is Gubler--Jell--Rabinoff semipositive}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The complete proof is \Cref{thm:p01-real-pl-positive-current-candidate}.
It uses a projective model of the reduction of the germ and an ample line
bundle $A$ on that model.  The integral PL germ realizing $A$ dominates
each member of the finite integral-PL decomposition of $h$ in both signs.
Rational approximation inside this order interval reduces the assertion to
the integral metric criterion \cite[Corollary~18.8.8]{CLD25}; nefness is
then closed because degrees on every proper integral curve pass to the
limit.

The exact pure-dimensional statement and proof passed production Rethlas
run \nolinkurl{20260825T080059Z_80f35689475f}, item
\nolinkurl{pi_33f9d15994f62f668065256e}, using
\texttt{gpt-5.6-sol} at \texttt{xhigh}, with final verdict
\texttt{correct}, zero critical errors and zero gaps.  An earlier run of a
broader wording is preserved but does not control the book: CLD introduce
curvature currents on $n$-spaces, hence on pure-dimensional analytic
spaces.  A bare non-pure-dimensional variant does not specify a single CLD
current bidegree and is not counted as a residual open problem.

The earlier curve-slicing work remains useful independently.
\Cref{prop:verified-lci-current-slice} proves the complete-intersection
slice inequality.  Moreover, \cite[Theorem~18.4.7]{CLD25} supplies the
degree--atom formula on arbitrary pure one-dimensional analytic spaces,
including singular and nonreduced ones; smoothness of a lifted detecting
curve is therefore unnecessary for that particular step.  Neither result
is needed in the ample-order-unit proof above, and no pullback operation for
an arbitrary positive current is asserted.

\subsection{Regularizing arbitrary classical psh functions}

\begin{problem}\label{prob:frontier-classical-regularization}
On which higher-dimensional good strict analytic spaces is every classically
psh function locally a decreasing limit of semipositive real PL, locally
Fubini--Study, weakly smooth psh, or CLD-smooth psh functions?
\end{problem}

The four targets must be separated.  Real PL functions on the relative
interior satisfy the three-way comparison of
\Cref{thm:verified-pl-psh-equivalence}.  On smooth boundaryless curves,
\cite[Proposition~15.11]{GJR26} gives decreasing weakly smooth
regularization locally on each relatively compact open subset.  Wanner's
published CLD-smooth regularization had the additional residue-field or curve
hypotheses stated in \cite[Corollary~5.4]{Wanner19};
\Cref{thm:p063-current-psh-ordinary-regularization} removes them for
continuous current-psh functions on smooth proper algebraic curves.
Weakly smooth harmonic functions need not be CLD-smooth.

The attempted higher-dimensional proof combines local formal models,
regularized maxima, and harmonic tropicalizations.  Curvewise approximation
does not by itself glue: the approximants must be compatible on overlapping
tropical charts and after scalar extension.  Nor may a nonmetrizable net be
replaced by a sequence without a countable extraction argument.  The general
problem is \emph{open}; the curve and PL cases are verified boundary cases.

There is a strictly invariant higher-dimensional semipositive-real-PL
endpoint as well.  On an ordinary open convex chamber of a split torus, a
finite continuous maximal-compact-torus-invariant psh function descends to a
finite convex tropical potential.  On every displayed good strictly analytic
inverse image of a nonempty ordinary open set compactly contained in the
chamber, finite tangent-plane approximations of gently shifted
radial smoothings give one decreasing semipositive real-PL sequence.  The
explicit pullbacks are CLD-psh, hence classically psh, and the real-PL
comparison then gives semipositivity without separatedness, boundarylessness,
or pure-dimensionality.  This begins with the invariant current-psh class,
not every classically psh function.  Its real-PL conclusion by itself does
not identify the sequence as locally Fubini--Study or weakly smooth; the two
separate companion arguments below add those regularities.

Their maxima are locally Fubini--Study and retain a quantitative

## Exact result and boundary

The requested all-obstacle triangle-square contact theorem is false. On the exact unit-weight graph and actual lattice specified in the assignment, the functions constructed below satisfy
\[
 P_\gamma(u)=\gamma\in\mathrm{PAPC}_{\mathbb R}(G^2,\gamma)
 \subset\mathrm{PC}_{\mathrm{reg},\mathbb R}(G^2,\gamma),\qquad
 \int_{G^2}(P_\gamma(u)-\gamma-u)\,
           \mathrm{MA}_{\mathrm{poly},\mathbb R}(P_\gamma(u))=-8.
 \tag{1}
\]
Here the reference is actual PC and positive at infinity, the obstacle is bounded real PA on finite rational spatial domains, and the raw competitors need not be continuous. This is an actual operator-domain counterexample, with exact envelope equality and a complete negative integral, rather than a regularity-failure alternative or an apparent local atom.

The original P05.2 task is the classification of arbitrary balanced pairs having the contact identity for every admissible obstacle. That classification remains open. In particular, this note does not classify every reference on this graph product, establish all-obstacle regularity for it, settle two arbitrary finite graphs, or address P06.2. Status is partial and candidate is false. The proposed conditional all-obstacle contact gate, even restricted to raw envelopes already in rational real PAPC on this triangle square, is also refuted by (1).

The difference-norm trap on two conical three-ray stars appears in the earlier round-06 draft. Its local calculation is reconstructed here and is not claimed as a new local mechanism. The new result is its actual global realization on the two bounded cyclic graphs, with the required positive-growth reference, raw-envelope comparison for all competitors and remote endpoints, and full recursive negative integral. No result, verdict, receipt or hash from that draft or the predecessor is a premise. This counterexample differs from the predecessor's imposed-contact positive example: its witnessed noncontact vertex has strictly positive complete recursive mass.

## Definitions and source obligations

The controlling source is Chapter 72 of the book, `parts/part6/ch72_major_open_problems.tex`, especially the polyhedral section, and its named Appendix M, `appendices/appM_ch18_frontiers.tex`. The active P05.2 requirement is the exact contact integral for all admissible obstacles; positive growth, balancing and total mass do not suffice. Chapter 72 explicitly leaves arbitrary nonseparable product obstacles and the higher-dimensional real PA case open. Appendix M concerns the analytic zero-current/classical pluriharmonic bridge and supplies no polyhedral product theorem used here.

We use Botero--Mazzon--Pille-Schneider, *Monge--Ampère measures on balanced polyhedral spaces*, arXiv:2603.08664v1, manuscript dated 10 March 2026 (BMPS), solely to fix the following definitions and normalization. Every mathematical implication used for the counterexample is proved below.

* A finite rational spatial complex consists of finitely many rational polyhedra meeting in common faces, with their faces included. A rational polyhedron can be defined by integer affine inequalities after clearing denominators (Definitions 2.1--2.4).
* For a face \(\sigma\), its actual saturated tangent lattice is \(N_\sigma=N\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\sigma-\sigma)\). For a facet \(\tau\prec\sigma\), a normal lift \(n_{\sigma/\tau}\) represents the primitive positive generator of \(N_\sigma/N_\tau\), pointing into \(\sigma\) (Definition 2.18). A real cycle is balanced when \(\sum_{\sigma\succ\tau}w_\sigma n_{\sigma/\tau}\in N_{\tau,\mathbb R}\) at every tested facet (Definitions 2.19--2.20, explicitly extended from rational to real weights here).
* A real PA function is continuous and real affine on a finite **rational spatial** structure. This is the real span of the literal integral-slope/rational-constant functions on that structure: continuity is a rational linear system, its real solution space has a rational basis, and clearing each basis vector's slope denominators makes it literal PA. Definition 2.28 itself is literal, not this extension. Real coefficients never permit irrational spatial walls in this note. Our actual example has rational coefficients throughout.
* A PCC consists of finitely many rational endpoints \(x_i\in X\cap N_{\mathbb Q}\), real \(\alpha_i\geq0\) summing to one, and the actual centre \(x=\sum_i\alpha_i x_i\). For some allowed rational structure there are faces \(\tau\preceq\sigma_i\) with \(x\in\tau\) and \(x_i\in\sigma_i\) (Definition 3.2). A finite raw PC function satisfies \(q(x)\leq\sum_i\alpha_iq(x_i)\) for every such PCC, on every allowed structure (Definition 3.3). We do not assume continuity of raw competitors.
* PAPC means that \(a\cdot z\geq0\) for every nonnegative real balanced local \(k\)-cycle, every \(k\geq1\), on every ordinary open subset (Definition 3.1 with the explicit real extension). ## Divisor algebra with actual primitive normals

For a real PA function \(a\) and balanced real \(k\)-cycle \(z\), the divisor is
\[
 (a\cdot z)(\tau)=
 \sum_{\sigma\succ\tau}z(\sigma)a_{\sigma,\mathrm{lin}}(n_{\sigma/\tau})
 -a_{\tau,\mathrm{lin}}
       \left(\sum_{\sigma\succ\tau}z(\sigma)n_{\sigma/\tau}\right).
 \tag{2}
\]
The last argument is tangent by balancing. Altering a lift by a tangent vector makes the two terms change equally, since the linear parts agree tangentially. The formula is therefore lift-independent, real bilinear and local on ordinary opens. Ambient affine functions have zero divisor.

Refinement compatibility in the dimensions needed here follows directly from (2). At a new tested facet, take its minimal old face. If that old face has dimension larger than the cycle dimension, every inherited incident weight is zero. If it has the cycle dimension, exactly two nonzero inherited pieces meet in that plane with equal weights and affine parts and opposite quotient normals, so their terms cancel. If it has the tested facet dimension, the tangent lattice and incident primitive normal classes are the old ones, and the coefficient is inherited unchanged. Extra incident pieces have zero inherited weight. These cases also preserve balancing of a subdivided cycle. Applying the same argument successively to the first divisor proves refinement compatibility of the second divisor. In particular, inserting vertices in an affine edge produces opposite slopes with identical edge weights and coefficient zero; inserting a vertex inside an affine top cell produces zero first divisor there.

For completeness, balancing of the first divisor of a two-cycle is also elementary. Translate the tested vertex to zero and use a pointed rational local two-fan; harmless rational cuts can make any local lineality pointed. Let \(r,s\) be the primitive boundary vectors of a two-cone. Its saturated plane lattice \(N_C\) has index
\[
 \chi_{rs}=[N_C:\mathbb Zr+\mathbb Zs].
\]
The primitive quotient normal at \(r\) is represented modulo \(\mathbb Rr\) by \(s/\chi_{rs}\): extend primitive \(r\) to a basis of \(N_C\), in which the transverse coordinate of \(s\) has absolute value \(\chi_{rs}\). The representative need not itself be an integral lift; their tangential difference cancels in (2). If cone weights are \(\omega_{rs}\), top balancing gives
\[
 \sum_{C_{rs}\succ r}\frac{\omega_{rs}}{\chi_{rs}}s=t_r r,
 \qquad
 D_a(r)=\sum_{C_{rs}\succ r}\frac{\omega_{rs}}{\chi_{rs}}a(s)-t_ra(r).
 \tag{3}
\]
Here \(a\) is the homogeneous germ after subtracting its value at the vertex. Multiplying \(D_a(r)\) by \(r\) and summing, the first sum is the sum, once for each unordered cone, of
\(\omega_{rs}(a(s)r+a(r)s)/\chi_{rs}\). Replacing \(t_rr\) by its balancing sum in the subtracted term gives exactly the same sum. Thus \(\sum_rD_a(r)r=0\), proving that the first divisor is a real one-cycle. Its complete second coefficient at the vertex is
\[
                      (a^2\cdot[X])\{0\}=\sum_rD_a(r)a(r).
 \tag{4}
\]
This includes every first-divisor face, including original branching axes and newly created diagonal faces.

The normalization is the intersection normalization. On a unit-weight complete plane, \(a(s,t)=|s|+|t|\) has first weight two on each of the four coordinate rays and germ value one on each primitive ray. Formula (4) gives eight, which is \(2!\) times the area four of the slope square. We use (2)--(4) themselves, not an Alexandrov substitution at singular junctions.

## Carrier, functions, and admissibility

Let \(G\subset\mathbb R^2\) be the triangle with
\[
 A=(0,0),\quad B=(1,0),\quad C=(0,1),
\]
the primitive bounded oriented edges \(A\to B=(1,0)\), \(B\to C=(-1,1)\), \(C\to A=(0,-1)\), each of primitive length one, and leaves \((-1,-1)\), \((2,-1)\), \((-1,2)\) at \(A,B,C\), respectively. All weights are one. The outgoing vectors at the three junctions are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 A&(1,0)&(0,1)&(-1,-1)\\
 B&(-1,0)&(-1,1)&(2,-1)\\
 C&(0,-1)&(1,-1)&(-1,2).
\end{array}
\]
Every row sums to zero, has rank two, and contains a determinant-one pair. Thus the graph is balanced in the actual saturated lattice \(\mathbb Z^2\); every local relation cone is generated by the strictly positive vector \((1,1,1)\). No lattice change or unfolding of the bounded cycle occurs.

Set \(X=G\times G\subset\mathbb R^4\), with coordinates \((x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)\), actual lattice \(N=\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z^2\), and unit product weights. There are thirty-six top product edge cells. Their tangent plane lattice is the direct sum of the two primitive factor edge lattices. At a codimension-one product face, balancing is the corresponding graph balancing sum with the other factor fixed. Hence \(X\) is a pure two-dimensional finite rational balanced space with precisely the required product weights.

In the pointed quotient, the sum of defining nonnegative forms is positive away from zero; its section of value one is bounded, since an unbounded sequence normalized on the sphere would produce a nonzero vector of value zero. A bounded polyhedron is the convex hull of its vertices: a line through a nonvertex point in its minimal face terminates in smaller faces, and induction reduces to vertices. Vertices solve full-rank active systems and are rational for rational data. Lift back and add both signs of a rational lineality basis. Homogenization therefore gives, for each nonempty pointed rational polyhedron,

σ=conv(A_σ)+cone(R_σ),

with finite rational point and ray sets. The corresponding real-data statement holds without coordinate rationality.

Elimination of a variable from finitely many nonstrict inequalities compares every lower bound with every upper bound and retains the inequalities independent of that variable. A one-sided family imposes no extra condition. Induction proves that polyhedral projections are polyhedra. Variable coefficients remain rational when initially rational, even with real constant terms. Applying this to convex-combination and cone variables also proves that finite convex-hull-plus-cone sets are closed.

All separations used here follow from nearest points. A point outside a nonempty closed convex set has a nearest point after compact restriction; differentiation of squared distance along segments gives a separating normal. A disjoint compact convex set and closed convex set have positive attained distance, and differentiation in both sets strictly separates them by their nearest-point difference. For a cone, a finite supremum of the separating functional is zero. Thus the point/cone and compact-polytope/cone separations used below need no external separation theorem.

A finite rationally convex function on Q^n has a unique continuous convex completion to R^n. Rational box corner values bound it above; reflection about a rational centre c gives F(y)≥2F(c)−F(2c−y), a lower bound on a smaller box. Choose L≤F≤M on c+[-2R,2R]^n. For rational y,z in c+[-R/2,R/2]^n, put δ=||z−y||∞. When δ>0, T=R/δ≥1 is rational and y+T(z−y) stays in the larger box. Jensen gives F(z)−F(y)≤(M−L)δ/R; reverse y,z for the opposite inequality. This proves local Lipschitz completion, and density proves convexity and uniqueness. The same argument proves continuity of a finite everywhere-defined convex function.

Such a function has an affine support at every point. Separate a point just below its closed epigraph by a nearest-point normal. Its vertical coefficient is positive: coefficient zero would give a nonzero horizontal functional bounded on all R^n. Normalize to obtain affine minorants with values approaching F(x) at x. Evaluating at x±Re_i bounds their slopes. A convergent subsequence gives a touching support. This includes dimension zero.

For a compact polyhedron D, its outward normal cone N_D(p) is generated by its active inequality normals. One inclusion follows from the inequalities. If a normal is outside that finitely generated closed cone, separation produces a direction satisfying active inequalities and increasing the alleged normal. A sufficiently small step also satisfies inactive inequalities, contradicting normality. Rational inequality normals therefore give rational normal-cone generators, even with real constants.

For a concave polyhedral function a(p)=min_i(c_i+g_i(p)), its supergradient polytope is the convex hull of active gradients g_i. Its directional derivative is their minimum; separation proves the supergradient assertion. Expanding finite minima shows that supergradients of nonnegative sums are the corresponding weighted Minkowski sums, including zero coefficients.

Primitive-normal algebra and normalization.

Use N_σ=N∩span_R(σ−σ), the actual saturated tangent lattice. For τ a facet of σ, choose an inward lift n_{σ/τ} of the primitive positive generator of N_σ/N_τ. For real PA a and a balanced real k-cycle z,

(a·z)(τ)=Σ_{σ>τ}z(σ)a_σ(n_{σ/τ})−a_τ(Σ_{σ>τ}z(σ)n_{σ/τ}).  (A)

The second sum is tangential. Normal-lift changes cancel because affine pieces agree on τ. The formula is bilinear and local on ordinary opens, and every ambient affine function has zero divisor.

For refinement, inspect the minimal old face containing a new tested (k−1)-face. If its dimension is k, the two inherited pieces have equal weight and linear part and opposite quotient normals, hence cancel. If its dimension is k−1, saturated tangents and incident primitive normal classes agree with the old ones. If its dimension exceeds k, inherited k-weights vanish. These cases prove refinement invariance. The same cancellation proves inherited balancing.

For balancing of the new divisor and commutativity, quotient at a (k−2)-face by its saturated tangent lattice and subtract ambient extensions of common tangential parts. Rational cuts make the resulting two-cones pointed. For a cone bounded by primitive rays r,s, use the actual index

χ_rs=[N_C:Zr+Zs].

Extending r to a basis of the saturated plane shows that the primitive inward normal modulo Rr is s/χ_rs. Quotient tangents remain saturated, since membership of a multiple in a rational tangent subspace forces membership of the original class. Writing ω_rs for the cone weight, balancing at r is

Σ_{C_rs>r}(ω_rs/χ_rs)s=t_r r.

The divisor coefficient is

D_a(r)=Σ_{C_rs>r}(ω_rs/χ_rs)a(s)−t_r a(r).
