which is symmetric. This proves balancing and commutativity for real coefficients and weights, in every germ. No primitive index is discarded.

Direct product lattices split primitive normals, so a divisor pulled back from one factor equals its divisor there times the other cycle. As a normalization check, Σ_{i=1}^d|s_i| on lattice-coordinate affine d-space of weight c has mass 2^d d!c at the origin: each coordinate occurs once in the expansion. No division by d! occurs anywhere in this argument.

Scalar graph facts without PC locality.

The strictly positive vector in K_v implies that the full kernel of the direction map has dimension one. Otherwise a small perturbation of that vector by another kernel vector stays positive, contradicting the hypothesis. At a bivalent vertex the primitive directions are opposite and weights equal. At larger valence there is no opposite pair, since it would give a second nonnegative relation. Rational edge subdivision preserves the hypothesis.

A convex polyhedron contained in G×E has convex projection into G. A straight segment cannot traverse a branching vertex, since no opposite pair is present. Its projection therefore lies in one straight chain through bivalent vertices, or in a vertex. This applies to arbitrary permitted structures.

Suppose k is finite on rational graph points and satisfies rational graph PCCs with rational coefficients. Complete it on each edge interior using rational Jensen. Its one-sided endpoint limit is finite and at most its endpoint value: endpoint secants bound it above and interior secants bound it below. For small rational t>0, the endpoints v+t v_{v,e}, with coefficients w_e/Σw_e, form an actual PCC. The inequality and endpoint upper bounds force every limit to equal k(v). Outgoing derivatives are bounded above by finite secants. Dividing the same PCC inequality by t prevents any derivative from being −∞ and proves

Σ_e w_e k′_e(v+)≥0.  (B)

Thus k has a continuous edgewise-convex completion and finite outgoing derivatives.

Conversely, a continuous edgewise-convex k satisfying (B), plus any affine function of E, satisfies every actual cylinder PCC. Bivalent inequalities give ordinary convexity on straight chains. At a branching centre v, group graph displacements as t_i v_{v,e}, t_i≥0. Their weighted sum vanishes; hence b_e=Σ_{i in e}α_i t_i=cw_e for c≥0. Edge convexity gives k(q_i)−k(v)≥t_i k′_e(v+), and summation gives Jensen by (B). At a centre in a straight chain this is ordinary convexity. Zero graph displacements and affine E terms follow from the barycentre identity. This covers real coefficients, all real centres, remote endpoints, and structures crossing artificial bivalent subdivisions.

For a raw cylinder function h and real p∈E*, define on rational graph points

k_{h,p}(q)=inf_{z∈E_Q}(h(q,z)−p(z)).  (C)

This satisfies rational graph PCCs: choose rational z_i approaching endpoint infima, use the actual cylinder PCC at (q,Σα_i z_i), subtract p, and take infima. Rational coefficients keep this barycentre rational. If an endpoint infimum is −∞, vary that endpoint alone.

If (C) is finite at one rational graph point, it is finite throughout that connected component. From an edge-interior centre, any other rational point on the edge can be an endpoint of a rational combination by choosing the other endpoint on the opposite side. At a vertex, any chosen remote rational endpoint v+t_e v_{v,e} belongs to a positive vertex PCC using rational coefficients proportional to w_e/t_e and small positive rational distances on the other edges. A finite centre precludes any endpoint value −∞. Propagation across the finite graph includes cycles and all ends. The preceding scalar completion then applies.

Finite obstacle data and exact tails.

Work componentwise and identify E rationally with its lattice vector space. Take a common finite rational structure for f=γ+u and γ, refined by original edge strips. Every cell is pointed: a lineality vector would yield two opposite reference recession slopes, incompatible with positivity at infinity.

\section{Detailed regularity and descent results}
\label{sec:appM-regularity-results}

Classical pluriharmonicity is defined by curve tests after arbitrary ground
field extension and therefore does not visibly provide a finite local
presentation by logarithms of analytic units.  On the quasi-smooth locus,
altered local uniformization and rigid $\acute{e}$tale descent remove this
gap.  The descent step is included because the uniformizing cover need not be
finite, flat, or boundaryless, so finite-flat descent cannot be applied to it
directly.

pluriharmonic regularity problem.  It is local on $X$: global

\Cref{prop:p061-integral-pl-counterexample}, the conclusion cannot be

The same conclusion has a finite-flat cover descent that is independent of

\begin{corollary}[Finite-flat cover descent for classical pluriharmonic regularity]
\label{cor:p061-finite-flat-cover-descent}
Let $K$ be a complete nontrivially valued field and let
$\pi:Y\to X$ be a finite, flat, surjective morphism of good strictly
$K$-analytic spaces.  Suppose that every classically pluriharmonic
function on every ordinary open subspace of $Y$ is $\mathbf R$-PL.
Then every classically pluriharmonic function on every ordinary open subspace
of $X$ is $\mathbf R$-PL and Gubler--Jell--Rabinoff harmonic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $U$ be an ordinary open subspace of $X$, let
$h\in\operatorname{PH}(U)$, and fix $x\in U$.  Choose a good strict
affinoid neighbourhood $U_0\subseteq U$ of $x$.  The restricted map
\[
 \pi^{-1}(U_0)\longrightarrow U_0
\]
is finite, flat, and surjective between good strictly $K$-analytic
spaces.  Classical pluriharmonicity is stable under analytic pullback
\cite[Proposition~7.2(6)]{GR25Classical}, so $\pi^*h$ is
$\mathbf R$-PL on $\pi^{-1}(U_0)$ by hypothesis.  Apply
\cite[Proposition~5.11]{GJR26} with the divisible coefficient group
$\Lambda=\mathbf R$.  It descends $\mathbf R$-PL regularity to
$h|_{U_0}$.  Since $x$ was arbitrary, $h$ is $\mathbf R$-PL on
$U$.

Both $h$ and $-h$ are classically psh.  The real-PL comparison
\cite[Theorem~4.3]{GR25Classical} makes both signs semipositive, which is
exactly Gubler--Jell--Rabinoff harmonicity.
\end{proof}

Consequently every ordinary neighbourhood admitting a finite flat surjective
cover by one of the verified P06.1 regularity ranges is itself in that
which assigns to any d-tuple in PCreg (X, γ) a positive Radon measure on X of total mass deg(γ)
(Definition 4.5), extends the polyhedral Monge–Ampère operator on PAPC functions, and is
continuous along decreasing sequences of regularizable PC functions.

   We establish two comparison results. First, for any PCreg function ϕ and for any maximal-
dimensional face of X, the polyhedral Monge–Ampère measure MApoly (ϕ, . . . , ϕ) (which we will
simply denote by MApoly (ϕ)) coincides with the real Monge–Ampère measure of the restriction of
ϕ to that face; see Proposition 4.20. Second, when X has dimension one, the operator MApoly on
piecewise smooth PC functions agrees with the (unbounded version of the) Laplacian operator as
defined by Baker and Faber in [BF06]; see Proposition 6.17.
  Finally, we further extend the polyhedral Monge–Ampère operator to the space PSH(X, γ) (see
Definition 4.21) and introduce an energy functional
                                     E : PSH(X, γ) → R ∪ {−∞}
defined as an antiderivative of the Monge–Ampère operator, in analogy with the complex setting.
This leads to the notion of γ-plurisubharmonic functions with finite energy, denoted by E 1 (X, γ);
see Definition 5.8.

1.3. The polyhedral Monge–Ampère equation. We now turn our attention to the polyhedral
Monge–Ampère equation, namely the problem of finding solutions to MApoly (·) = µ for a given
measure µ on X. Inspired by the variational approaches developed in [Ber+13] and [BFJ15] in
the complex and non-archimedean settings respectively, we introduce a functional Fµ on the space
PSH(X, γ) and study conditions on the pair (X, γ) under which a maximizer of Fµ yields a solution
to the polyhedral Monge–Ampère equation.
    The functional Fµ is defined in terms of the energy functional E, and the variational method
relies on suitable differentiability properties of E, in particular of its composition with the envelope
Pγ (Definition 6.2). To this end, in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 we introduce two structural properties
of the pair (X, γ), which we call regularity and orthogonality in analogy with the complex and
non-archimedean settings, and prove the following result.
Theorem 1.3 (Proposition 6.12). Assume that (X, γ) has the regularity and orthogonality
properties. For any compactly supported Radon measure µ on X, the functional Fµ admits a
maximizer ϕ ∈ PSH(X, γ), which is a solution to MApoly (ϕ) = µ. Moreover if γ is strictly convex,
then ϕ ∈ PCreg (X, γ).

   The regularity property implies in particular the equality PC(X, γ) = PCreg (X, γ); see
Theorem 6.4. This property is satisfied in dimension one (Proposition 6.13), by complete polyhedral
spaces, and by conical polyhedral spaces where one considers conical PC functions; see Remark 6.6.
The validity of the orthogonality property appears to be more delicate: we exhibit counterexamples
already in dimension one, as well as in the special case of Bergman fans when γ is not strictly convex;
see Section 6.5. While such properties cannot be expected to hold for arbitrary balanced polyhedral
spaces, determining the extent to which regularity and orthogonality are satisfied, and clarifying

their geometric meaning, therefore appears as a natural problem that is likely to play a central role

PSH(X, γ) solving the Monge–Ampère equation MApoly (ϕ) = µ. Moreover if γ is strictly convex,
then ϕ ∈ PCreg (X, γ).
